notesStmt.note: Horace Traubel reprints a letter from Henry M. Alden, dated 12 May 1885, in which the Harper's editor rejects "Fancies at Navesink" as not likely to "make a favorable impression upon our readers" (With Walt Whitman in Camden [Boston: Small, Maynard & Company, 1906] 1:61). Whitman created his manuscript, then, at some point prior to that date, but more precise dating is difficult, as it represents a very early draft stage and because the many extant "Fancies at Navesink" suggest a longer than usual composition process for those poems.

These trial phrases and lines contributed to the poem "Last of Ebb, and Daylight Waning," part of the eight-poem sequence "Fancies at Navesink," first published in the August 1885 issue of Nineteenth Century.
